title: London After Midnight

evidence.note: Published 1927 by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer; the US copyright was renewed in its 28th year by Loew's Inc. and, under the Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act, ran for 95 years total from the publication date, expiring at the end of 2022. The film entered the public domain in the United States on January 1, 2023, as confirmed by Duke CSPD's Public Domain Day 2023 listing.
evidence.source: Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain — Public Domain Day 2023

evidence.note: London After Midnight is a silent film. The 1927 original carried no synchronized recorded score; at contemporary screenings, musicians compiled accompaniments from pre-existing classical works. No protected sound recording is attached to the original print. The only accessible moving-image version today is the 2002 TCM photographic reconstruction produced by Rick Schmidlin; that version was issued with a newly recorded musical accompaniment. Under US copyright law any score or sound recording added to a modern presentation of a silent film is independently protected, making the audio layer of the reconstruction off-limits for reuse even though the underlying silent images are public domain.

The story 'The Hypnotist' is an original work by director Tod Browning, created for this film and not adapted from any previously published source; the scenario was written by Waldemar Young from Browning's story, with titles by Joseph W. Farnham. The work was first published as part of the 1927 film. No prior or separate publication of 'The Hypnotist' as a standalone text is known, and no separate unpublished-work copyright registration was identified in this session. The film's 95-year US copyright term has expired; the underlying scenario is in the public domain.
evidence.source: Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain — Public Domain Day 2023; Wikipedia, 'London After Midnight (film)' (production credits confirmed)

trademark.note: The 'Man in the Beaver Hat' — Lon Chaney's top-hatted, sharp-toothed figure — is a well-known piece of horror iconography from this film. Warner Bros. Discovery (successor to Turner Entertainment and the MGM catalog) may assert commercial rights to this imagery. No active trademark registration for the character design or the film title was confirmed during this research session; reusers in commercial contexts should conduct independent trademark clearance before using that specific character likeness.

evidence.note: A 45-minute photographic reconstruction was produced in 2002 by Rick Schmidlin for Turner Classic Movies, using surviving 1927 production stills with added camera motion effects. The underlying still photographs, dating from 1927, are in the public domain. The reconstruction's original creative expression — the selection and arrangement of stills, the applied camera motion, and any accompanying musical recording — constitutes independently copyrightable authorship dating from 2002 and is not freed by the print's public-domain status. Under Bridgeman v. Corel (S.D.N.Y. 1999), a faithful reproduction of a public-domain work adds no new copyright, but original creative choices in assembly do. Ripping the reconstruction from a copy-protected disc may also implicate 17 U.S.C. § 1201 regardless of the underlying work's status.

editorial:
London After Midnight is a 1927 American silent mystery-horror produced by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer and directed by Tod Browning, with Lon Chaney in the lead. Its story, 'The Hypnotist,' was an original creation by Browning, adapted for the screen by Waldemar Young with titles by Joseph W. Farnham. The film's US copyright — renewed in its 28th year by Loew's Inc. — ran 95 years total and expired at the end of 2022, placing the film and its underlying scenario in the public domain as of January 1, 2023. A creator wanting to adapt the premise, remake it, or publish the scenario has a clear runway: no prior published work underlies the story, and the copyright term is definitively expired.

The practical obstacle is that no original print survives. The film is one of cinema's most sought-after lost works; only production stills remain after a 1965 MGM vault fire destroyed the last known print. The only accessible version is the 2002 TCM photographic reconstruction produced by Rick Schmidlin, which assembles surviving stills with applied camera motion. The reconstruction's original creative elements — its assembly choices and any accompanying musical recording — carry their own copyright and are not freed by the print's public-domain status. A reuser drawing from the reconstruction rather than from original 1927 production stills is working with material that is only partially free.
faq: Can I use footage from London After Midnight?

No original footage exists — the film is completely lost. The only accessible moving-image version is the 2002 TCM photographic reconstruction produced by Rick Schmidlin, which is itself a separately copyrighted work. The underlying 1927 story and any surviving original production stills are public domain and free to use, but the reconstruction as assembled is not.
Can I remake or adapt this story?

Yes. The story 'The Hypnotist' by Tod Browning was created for and first published as part of the 1927 film; no prior or independent publication of that story is known, and its copyright term has expired along with the film's. You can adapt the scenario and characters freely. Note that the 'Man in the Beaver Hat' character design may carry separate trademark interest by Warner Bros. Discovery as successor to MGM; conduct a trademark search before using that specific character likeness in a commercial context.
